newsitem.title: KENYA: Drought forces Kenya to import maize.
newsitem.headline: Drought forces Kenya to import maize.

text.p: Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi has authorised the commercial import of maize for drought victims, the presidency said on Wednesday.
"President Moi has observed that many parts of the country were experiencing persistent drought and food shortages due to the failure by short and long rains," Moi's press service said.
"President Moi said (on Tuesday) the importation of more maize was to ensure the affected families were fed," it added.
The presidency did not say what amount of maize would be imported of where it would come from. There was also no word on how many people were facing food shortages due to the drought.

Early this month, the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) said it was asking donors for $12.4 million to buy 25,000 tonnes of maize, beans and vegetable oil to feed distressed people in north-eastern and eastern provinces for the next six months.
"The situation in 1997 is the most serious since the 1992/93 drought. If the next rains in March and April fail, we have a big problem," Mike Sackett, WFP's director in Kenya, said.
Moi's press agency said the presidency had issued food appeals and thanked countries that had responded positively. It did not say what food donations had so far been received.

Food distribution has begun or is about to begin to 270,000 primary school children in Eastern Province, which stretches up to the Ethiopian border, and to about 207,000 drought victims in North Eastern province, which borders on Somalia.
The arid north-east is Kenya's poorest and most thinly populated province. Food supply is precarious for the mainly pastoral nomadic people at the best of times.
The region has seen little development since independence from Britain in 1963 and the Somali conflict in the 1990s has flooded the province with immigrants and weapons.
Kenya's strategic food reserve is intended for use in precisely the circumstances now existing in the north.
WFP's Sackett said the government was drawing from the reserve to help out but it had shrunk to about 700,000 90-kg bags of maize from the target level of three million bags.
Donor sources monitoring Kenyan food stocks are alarmed about rising prices nationwide of maize, the staple for the 30 million population.
Because of last year's poor harvest and a 25 percent duty on imported maize there is currently a 500,000 tonne deficit, one analyst said.
